passage:
Vishal, you look worried about telling your mother you don't want to do the morning aarti anymore. Sit. Let your Avni Dadi tell you something.
I was fifteen when the prayers went hollow for me. Every evening my mother lit the lamp and sang, and I stood beside her feeling nothing. I thought I was a bad daughter. I was terrified of hurting her.
For months I pretended. Then one evening I just said it, holding her hand: "Ma, I don't feel what you feel when you pray. I'm sorry. I still want to stand with you, if that's allowed."
She was silent a long while. Then she said, "Stand with me, then. Maybe you'll feel it one day, maybe not." And I kept lighting the lamp for her every evening until she died.
So speak gently, Vishal, and keep being kind. That matters more than the words.

qa.q: How old was Avni when the prayers went hollow for her?
qa.a: Avni was fifteen when the prayers went hollow for her.

qa.q: How did Avni feel during the months she pretended?
qa.a: She felt empty during the prayers and terrified of hurting her mother, and she thought she was a bad daughter.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Avni's story?
qa.a: It came when she told her mother honestly and gently, holding her hand, while offering to keep standing with her; her kindness let her mother accept the doubt.

qa.q: How did Avni's mother seem to feel when she heard?
qa.a: She was silent a long while, likely hurt and surprised, but she chose acceptance, letting Avni stand with her without pretending.

grounding: An elder recalls doubting her family's rituals as a teenager, fearing to hurt her mother, and how honest, gentle words and continued kindness helped them adjust.

It was the last week of Ramadan and the week of Zainab's pre-board exams. At four a.m., Ammi woke her for sehri as always, and Zainab, sixteen, sat at the table half asleep, eating dates for a fast she no longer believed in.
She'd felt it for a year: the prayers were words she knew by heart but no longer felt. She had told only her friend Elizabeth, who just listened.
That morning, Ammi said, "You look so tired. Is the fast too much with exams?"
Instead of just saying yes, Zainab said quietly, "Ammi, it's not just the exams. I don't feel it the way you do anymore. I don't want to lie to you."
Ammi's hand stopped on the teapot. Her eyes filled.
"I still want to sit with you at sehri," Zainab added. "Every morning. I love this time with you."
After a long moment, Ammi poured her tea. "Then sit," she said softly.

qa.q: Whom had Zainab told about her doubts?
qa.a: She had told only her friend Elizabeth.

qa.q: What was Zainab afraid of before she spoke?
qa.a: Zainab was afraid of hurting Ammi, which is why she had kept her doubt hidden for a year.

qa.q: What made Zainab's words respectful?
qa.a: She spoke quietly and honestly without criticising the faith, and she offered to keep sitting with Ammi at sehri, showing her love continued.

qa.q: How was Ammi affected by Zainab's words?
qa.a: Ammi was shocked and hurt, her hand stopping and her eyes filling, but she chose to keep Zainab close, softly telling her to sit.

grounding: During exams and Ramadan, a teenager admits to her mother that the prayers have lost meaning, fearing to hurt her, and continued kindness helps them adjust.

passage:
Every morning at six, Manoj rang the brass bell in their Kolkata flat, and every morning Ankita, fifteen, stood behind him with folded hands, thinking about her chemistry test.
One Sunday, she didn't get up. Her father knocked. "Puja, Ankita?"
She came out slowly. "Baba, can I tell you something without you getting angry?"
He put down the bell.
"I've been standing there for months not feeling anything. I don't know if I believe. I didn't want to hurt you, so I kept pretending." Her voice shook.
Manoj looked at the little shrine for a long time. "I doubted too, at your age," he said finally. "Your Thakuma never knew."
"Will you be disappointed if I don't come every day?"
"I'll miss you there," he said. "But I'd rather have you honest. Come when you want. Make my tea after, at least?"
Ankita laughed shakily. "Every day."

qa.q: What time did Manoj ring the brass bell?
qa.a: Every morning at six.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when her voice shook?
qa.a: Ankita felt nervous and afraid of hurting her father after months of pretending.

qa.q: Which choice helped Ankita and her father stay close?
qa.a: Ankita spoke honestly and gently, and offered to keep making his tea, so her doubt didn't become distance.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel about Ankita skipping puja?
qa.a: Manoj feels a little sad, saying he'll miss her there, but he also understands because he doubted at her age and prefers her honesty.

grounding: A teenager tells her father that the rituals have lost meaning, fearing to hurt him, and respectful words and small kindnesses help him adjust.

passage:
At the temple fair in their small town, Siddharth, sixteen, carried trays for the stalls but didn't go inside to pray. His cousin Akash noticed.
"Oye, atheist! Lost soul!" Akash shouted, and his friends laughed. An aunt added, "No God means no morals. What will become of him?"
Siddharth's ears burned. He kept carrying trays.
Later, an old woman slipped near the steps, and Siddharth was the first to reach her. He helped her up, found her son, and fetched her water.
His grandfather had seen it all. At dinner he said, in front of everyone, "Nobody at this table shames the boy for his thoughts. I watched him today. He has more kindness than half the people who went inside."
Akash stared at his plate. The aunt said nothing. Siddharth didn't look up, but he smiled a little.

qa.a: He helped her up, found her son, and fetched her water.

qa.a: Siddharth felt ashamed and hurt, his ears burning, but he kept carrying trays.

qa.q: What did the grandfather do that protected Siddharth?
qa.a: He refused to let the family shame Siddharth's honest thoughts, and pointed to his kindness as proof that values do not depend on belief.

qa.q: How might Akash feel after the grandfather's words?
qa.a: Akash likely feels embarrassed and guilty, which is why he stares at his plate.

passage:
At the Friday Shabbat dinner in Haifa, Aunt Esther asked Yosef, fifteen, to say the blessing over the bread. He hesitated. "Can Grandpa do it? I don't really... believe it."
Esther put down her glass. "No faith, no values. That's how children end up lost."
The table went quiet. Yosef's face turned red. He said nothing.
After dinner, he washed every dish without being asked, and fished his little cousin's toy car out from under the sofa. His mother found him in the kitchen, jaw tight.
"You were honest," she said. "That took courage. Esther's afraid for you, but she was wrong to say it like that." She squeezed his shoulder. "Your kindness is your values, Yosef."
The next week, Esther called. "I shouldn't have said that," she admitted. "You were the only one who helped clean."

qa.q: What did Aunt Esther ask Yosef to do?
qa.a: She asked him to say the blessing over the bread.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling when his face turned red?
qa.a: Yosef felt ashamed and hurt after Esther said that no faith meant no values.

qa.q: How did Yosef's mother support him?
qa.a: She praised his honesty, said Esther was wrong to shame him, and told him his kindness showed his values.

qa.q: Why might Esther react differently a week later?
qa.a: She may have realised she was speaking from fear, and seeing Yosef help clean showed her his good conduct, so she felt sorry.

grounding: Outside India, a teenager who does not believe is shamed by a relative, and his kindness and his mother's support show that values do not depend on belief.

passage:
At the school assembly, Seema, fourteen, stood silently with her eyes open while everyone else prayed. Afterwards, in the corridor, two girls from her class blocked her way.
"We saw. You don't pray. My mother says people like you have no morals."
"You'll end up lost," said the other.
Seema's throat tightened. "I just don't believe. I'm not hurting anyone."
They laughed and walked off. Seema went into the washroom and stayed there until the bell.
Binita Ma'am, the class teacher, noticed her red eyes in the next period and asked her to stay back. Seema told her everything.
Binita Ma'am said, "Thank you for telling me. Believing or not believing is a private matter. You were honest and respectful in assembly. Nobody has the right to call you immoral." She spoke to the two girls that day, and asked Seema to tell her if it happened again.

qa.q: What did the two girls say their mother says?
qa.a: One said, "My mother says people like you have no morals."

qa.q: How did Seema feel after the girls walked off?
qa.a: Seema felt hurt and ashamed, her throat tight, and hid in the washroom until the bell.

qa.q: How did Binita Ma'am respond well?
qa.a: She noticed Seema's distress, listened, said belief is private and that Seema had been respectful, and spoke to the girls that day.

qa.q: What would change if Binita Ma'am had ignored Seema's red eyes?
qa.a: Seema might keep hiding and feel that her honest thoughts made her a bad person, and the teasing might continue.

grounding: At school, a teenager who does not pray is called immoral and lost by peers, and a teacher refuses to let her honest thought be shamed.

Exam week in the hostel, and the power had gone out again. Zubin, twenty, sat on his bed in the torch-light, retying the thin cord of his kusti around his waist as he did every morning and night.
From the next bed, someone snorted. "Still doing the magic string thing, Zubin? In the twenty-first century?" The others laughed.
Zubin's hands paused. His face went hot. He'd heard this before, since first year.
Then Hrithik, who didn't believe in anything and said so often, put down his notes. "Leave him. He sits with me every night explaining calculus. He's the most thoughtful guy on this floor."
"You don't even believe in God," someone said.
"No," Hrithik said. "And he does. We argue about it over chai. He's never once called me foolish."
Zubin finished the knot. Later, he offered Hrithik the last of his biscuits, and Hrithik took two.

qa.a: He was retying the thin cord of his kusti around his waist.

qa.a: Zubin felt embarrassed and hurt, his face going hot, because he had been mocked about it since first year.

qa.a: It shows respect running both ways: a non-believer can defend a believer, value his thoughtfulness, and disagree warmly over chai.

qa.a: Hrithik seems to value it deeply, feeling respected because Zubin has never called him foolish for his own views.

Every morning in the college hostel in Chennai, Anand, nineteen, drew a thin line of vibhuti on his forehead before class. By the second week, Pranav had a nickname for him: "Pandit-ji."
"Our physics genius still believes ash will help him pass," Pranav announced in the canteen. People laughed. Anand kept eating, but he started washing off the vibhuti before class.
A week later, Pranav was struggling with a lab report at midnight. Anand sat with him until two, patiently explaining every step.
At the end, Pranav said, "Why did you stop wearing the ash?"
Anand shrugged. "Got tired of the jokes."
Pranav was quiet. "I'm sorry. I thought believing meant not thinking. You clearly think more than me."
The next morning, the line of vibhuti was back. Pranav nodded at it, and said nothing.

qa.a: Pranav called him "Pandit-ji."

qa.a: Anand felt embarrassed and tired of the jokes, so he hid a part of his faith to avoid being mocked.

qa.a: Pranav first saw belief as a lack of thinking, but after Anand's patient help he apologises and quietly accepts the vibhuti, seeing Anand as thoughtful.

"Himani, you're fasting AGAIN? It's the third Navratri day. You know it doesn't actually do anything, right?"
"It does something for me, Pallavi."
"Like what? It's just superstition. You're a science student!"

I stopped believing when I was seventeen. I'm Ganga, and my family knows. But last month, when Nani asked me to sit beside her for the Satyanarayan puja, I said yes.
My cousin Yash raised an eyebrow. "You? At a puja?"
I told him the truth: "I'm not here for the gods. I'm here for Nani."
I sat cross-legged on the floor for two hours. I passed the flowers when the priest asked. I didn't chant the words I don't believe, but I listened to Nani's voice, cracked and certain, and I remembered being five and falling asleep in her lap during this same story.
When the prasad came round, Nani pressed extra into my hand. "I know you don't believe, beti," she said quietly. "I'm happy you came anyway."
I didn't have to pretend. That's what made it feel like home.

Hostel warden's note, Diwali evening.
The students organised the hostel's Lakshmi puja this year. Sachin, 20, second year, is known among the boys for saying openly that he doesn't believe in God, so I was surprised to see him there from four o'clock, arranging diyas along the corridor.
Preeti, from the girls' wing, asked him about it while they were stringing marigolds. I overheard his answer: "I don't pray. But my mother always made rangoli on Diwali, and this is the first year I'm away. I wanted it to look like home." He said it simply, without apology.
During the aarti he stood at the back and didn't join the chants, but he held the plate for the student who led it.
After, he stayed to sweep up the petals. I thanked him. Next step: I've asked him to help plan next year's festivals too.

Eid, 6 a.m.
Went to the Eidgah with Abbu and Tanvir this morning, like every year. I haven't prayed properly in two years. They both know. Last year I told Abbu, gently, "I don't believe the way you do, but I want to come."
Today Abbu handed me my old prayer mat anyway. I stood in the women's row with Ammi and my cousins. When they bowed, I stood still, hands folded, and just listened to thousands of people breathing together. It still gives me goosebumps.
Afterwards Tanvir, who is fourteen and dramatic, said, "You didn't even pray, Apa." Ammi said, "She came. That's enough." And then she hugged me longer than usual.
We ate sheer khurma at Nani's and I fed the little cousins. I don't believe, but I belong here. I don't have to lie to have both.
Sharmila

Mamu and I used to fight about God every Eid. He'd quote verses; I'd quote science. I'm Zainab, and I always "won," and he always left early.
This year my flatmate Tenzin, who meditates every morning though I've never seen her argue about it, gave me advice: "Stop trying to win. Ask him what it gives him."
So when Mamu started, I asked, "Mamu, when did your faith feel strongest?"
He was surprised. Then he told me about the year his first shop burned down, when he had three children and no money, and how praying at night was the only thing that stopped him from falling apart.
I didn't agree with his answers about the universe. I told him so. But I said, "I understand why it matters to you." He nodded.
We talked for two hours. He stayed for dinner. Neither of us changed our minds. It was the best Eid we'd had.

qa.q: What happened to Mamu's first shop?
qa.a: Mamu's first shop burned down.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel after hearing Mamu's story?
qa.a: Zainab felt moved and understanding, seeing the hope behind his faith even while still disagreeing.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin's advice work?
qa.a: Asking what faith gave Mamu, instead of scoring points, let Zainab hear the hope behind his belief, so both felt respected.

qa.a: Mamu likely felt respected and listened to, which is why he stayed for dinner instead of leaving early.

Facilitator's note, intergenerational dialogue circle, community centre, Sunday.
Chaitanya, 24, came with his grandmother, Irawati Aaji, who is 81. He has told the group before that he is an atheist; she is a lifelong devotee of the Warkari tradition.
Today's topic was "What gives life meaning?" I noticed that Chaitanya did not argue when Aaji spoke about the pilgrimage to Pandharpur. Instead he asked, "What did you feel the first time you walked it, Aaji?" She described walking for weeks as a young widow, with strangers who fed her.
When his turn came, he said he found meaning in science and in people, and that he didn't believe in the deity. Aaji listened without interrupting.
At the end, she said to the group, "He doesn't believe, but he asks good questions. That is a kind of respect." Chaitanya held her hand.
Next step: I invited them to lead next month's session together.

Long talk with Sharmila Mashi today. She's the only one in our family who says she doesn't believe in God, and I pray every morning, so we usually avoid the topic.
Today she asked me straight: "What do you actually get from praying, Kiran?" Old me would've got defensive. Instead I said, "Calm, mostly. And hope. When Baba was in hospital it was the only thing I could do." Then I asked her, "What do you lean on instead?" She said, "People. Walks. Music." She told me about her friends who got her through her divorce.
I didn't try to convince her, and she didn't try to convince me. At one point she said, "I don't agree, but I like how you think." I felt the same.
We ended up making tea at midnight and laughing about my cousin's wedding.
Minds unchanged. Hearts somehow closer.
Kiran

Sonali, you asked why your father knows so much about every religion. It was my doing. Sit.
I was twenty-five, a young mother in a railway colony, and your father was six. One day he came home from school crying because a boy said his friend Yusuf would "go to hell." He asked me, "Is that true, Ma?"
I didn't know how to answer. My family said only our way was right. So I decided: I would teach him about every faith fairly, and about people who believe in none.
Every Sunday, we read one story: from the Gita, the Bible, the Quran, the Guru Granth Sahib, the Buddha, and one about a scientist who didn't believe. He asked questions; I answered honestly, or said I didn't know.

It was nine at night, Shreya had a work call at six the next morning, and her daughter, six, still wouldn't sleep.
"Mumma, why does Afreen Aunty's family pray five times? And why don't we?"
Shreya, twenty-six, was exhausted. She almost said, "Just go to sleep." Then she remembered her own mother, who had answered every question about other faiths with "Don't ask."

Irfan and his wife had agreed on almost everything before their son was born, except this.
Now Ojas was five, and at his grandparents' houses he heard two different answers about God. Irfan's mother taught him the Kalma. His wife's mother taught him the Gayatri mantra. Ojas came home and asked, "Which one is mine?"
Irfan, twenty-six, sat on the balcony that night with his wife. "I don't want him to feel he has to choose to please one of them," he said. She agreed.
So they made a small plan: stories from both faiths, and from others too; honest answers to every question; and permission to say, "I'm not sure yet."
The next morning Ojas asked, "Is Nana-ji's God angry with Dadi's God?"
Irfan laughed and pulled him close. "No. People just pray in different ways. Ask me anything, anytime."
